title: Find the constant from the number of solutions
subtitle: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables  · 22 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **22 of the official questions in Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables  are this one** — 1 Easy, 5 Medium, 16 Hard.
It is top-heavy: most versions are Hard, so it only earns study time once your target actually requires that tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:

- You're told a quadratic contains an unknown constant and has exactly one solution, no real solutions, or more than one real solution, and you're asked for the constant, or the largest or smallest value it can take.
- Sometimes it's framed as a parabola meeting a horizontal line or another line exactly once.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Move everything to one side so it reads ax^2 + bx + c = 0, and read off a, b and c, which may still contain the constant.
- 2) Set b^2 - 4ac = 0 for exactly one solution, < 0 for none, or > 0 for two.
- If it has to be an integer, take the boundary integer on the correct side of the inequality.

sections.heading: Where Desmos fits
body: Type the equation with the constant as a slider, for example y = (left side) - (right side), and slide until the parabola just touches the x-axis (one solution) or clears it (none).
If it's a line meeting a parabola, graph both and slide until they're tangent.
You can also type b^2-4ac with the slider and read its sign.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: The equation isn't in standard form yet, so you read a, b or c off the wrong side, or you forget the minus sign when moving a term.
On inequality versions you also get the direction wrong (< 0 means none, > 0 means two) or pick the integer just outside the allowed range.
